newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU takes final step to protect stock investors.
newsitem.headline: EU takes final step to protect stock investors.

text.p: The European Union put the final seal on Wednesday on legislation to protect small stock investors when an investment firm goes bankrupt.

The new rules, expected to be incorporated into national laws by late 1998, foresee minimum compensation of 20,000 European currency units ($22,900) when a firm proves unable to refund investors' money or securities.
The directive was given the final go-ahead by the European Parliament, following approval by EU finance ministers on Monday.
Most EU countries already have guarantee funds run by national stock exchanges or stockbrokers but the level of cover varies widely.

Germany provides almost full protection and the French and British schemes also provide compensation that is higher than the EU's minimum. A few countries, however, have no legislation or are only just implementing it.
Initially proposed in 1993, the EU's investor compensation directive aims to boost investors' confidence now that investment firms can operate throughout the 15-nation bloc with a single licence.

"This long awaited measure will substantially reinforce the single market for securities trading by serving to increase investors' confidence," Mario Monti, the EU commissioner responsible for the European single market, said in a statement.
The directive is identical to another EU law protecting the interests of small depositors.

Both were strongly but unsuccessfully opposed by Germany, which contested two key provisions effectively allowing foreign branches to join its generous scheme and banning its own firms from exporting their high level of protection.
The controversial provisions, known as the "top-up" and "export-ban" clauses, were imposed by a majority of EU countries because of the need to provide a level playing field within national markets.

Germany asked the European Court of Justice to outlaw the deposits guarantee directive adopted in 1994, but the court's advocate-general Fernand Leger last December proposed that the request be rejected. The court generally follows the opinion of its advocates-general. ($1 = 0.87 Ecu)
